newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: AT LEAST 82 DEAD IN GUATEMALA STADIUM TRAGEDY.
newsitem.headline: AT LEAST 82 DEAD IN GUATEMALA STADIUM TRAGEDY.

text.p: At least 82 people were crushed to death in an avalanche of bodies at an overcrowded Guatemalan stadium after fans without tickets barged in to see a World Cup soccer qualifying game on Wednesday, witnesses and firemen said on Thursday.

The municipal fire department estimated "82 or 83 dead" at the Guatemala-Costa Rica game, with a final count still pending, a spokesman said on Thursday morning. It was the worst stadium disaster in World Cup history.
"Fans' faces were turning blue and purple," eyewitness Kimberly White, a Reuters photographer, said. "They couldn't breathe. I heard people screaming and screaming."
Guatemalan President Alvaro Arzu, who rushed onto the field with tears in his eyes to call off the match, declared three days of national mourning for the victims.

A Reuters correspondent counted 79 dead, including two children, lying on the field of the Mateo Flores stadium after the tragedy, dubbed the "black night" by local media. After the initial death toll early on Thursday, emergency workers reported that up to four more had died in local hospitals.
Bodies were lined up in a row on the running track surrounding the field in an improvised morgue. Victims' shoes, torn clothing and bloodstains littered the stands above.
Dazed and grieving relatives gathered outside hospitals to seek news of the dead and injured. Many still had their faces painted in the blue and white colours of the Guatemalan flag.
From the Vatican, Pope John Paul II sent his condolences to the victims, telling them he was "deeply saddened" by the tragedy and offering his prayers for the dead.

In a preliminary report submitted by a match commissioner who attended the game, FIFA, world soccer's governing body in Zurich, Switzerland, said forged tickets may have triggered the stampede. It said angry fans kicked down an entrance door to the south stands causing spectators inside to cascade down to the lower levels.
"The proper number of tickets was issued, 45,800, but we are going to investigate," Guatamalan soccer chief Rolando Pineda Lam told reporters.

Witnesses said gate-crashers pushing into the cheap stands from the street at the south end of the stadium overwhelmed fans below, causing a mass of people to tumble down on top of each other toward the playing field about half an hour before the game's scheduled start at 8 p.m. (0200 GMT on Thursday).
The south end entrance to the stadium is at street level, with the playing field and lower stands below ground.

Many died crushed against the chainlink fence separating the stands from the playing field. Emergency workers opened up the fence to relieve the pressure but too late to save people who had already suffocated.
Victims screamed in pain as rescue workers attended more than 100 fans, many blue and purple from lack of oxygen.
Alberto Chamale, a 46-year-old construction worker, limping and disorientated, told Reuters he had lost four brothers and a niece in the crush.

"There was no room for more people but more and more came in," he said. "There were too many people. They pushed us forward." Choking back tears, he said emergency workers told him his relatives were among the bodies laid out on the field.

Another fan, Carlos Garcia, fought back the pain of a broken leg as he told of the disaster. "I was in the stands but they were full," he said. "Then more people were let in. I only felt that they began to fall on top of us. I don't know anything more."
Some fans tried to perform mouth-to-mouth resuscitation on victims, helping about 15 overwhelmed firefighters. Crowds of people stood overhead, waving jackets to provide air.

Guatemalan officials said the stadium was packed well beyond its 45,800 capacity an hour before kickoff, with some estimating that up to 60,000 were in the facility, close to the centre of Guatemala City. The Mateo Flores stadium is a concrete 1940s bowl that serves as both the national stadium and the venue of the capital's leading soccer clubs.

Guatemala's attorney general, solicitor general and health minister all made public calls for a thorough investigation to determine who was responsible for the overcrowding. If found guilty of negligence in the disaster, the Guatemala Football Association could face possible FIFA sanctions.
